content: The most recent versions of specifications will be made available, while all evaluations will also be accessible. Specifications and evaluations are typically published as a single, two-part document. Evaluations provide the evidence and rationale upon which the Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) recommendations are based. These evaluations do not contain confidential information. The process of developing specifications and decisions based on such information is explained as thoroughly as possible while maintaining confidentiality. The content of evaluation reports and the style of publications are determined by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO). Proposers and data owners are usually identified in evaluations. However, proposers are not typically identified in specifications, except indirectly through references to the evaluation. In exceptional cases, and at the discretion of FAO or WHO, a proposer may be identified in a footnote to a specification if it is necessary to clarify which specification applies to that proposer. Withdrawn specifications no longer hold the status of FAO or WHO specifications, and their use for regulatory purposes is strongly discouraged. Analytical methods adopted or accepted by the Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) are usually first published under a pre-publication scheme before appearing in printed form in CIPAC Handbooks, CD-ROMs, or the AOAC (Association of Official Analytical Chemists) Handbook and Journal. Physical test methods are published in CIPAC Handbooks. Methods supporting WHO specifications developed under previous procedures are attached to the specifications. FAO and WHO will prepare a program to review all published specifications, which will be considered by the JMPS. As part of their product stewardship responsibilities and as a condition for maintaining an FAO or WHO specification, proposers must inform FAO/WHO of changes in the manufacturing process that affect the existing specification, as well as changes in company name or address. Specifications are published on the basis that information on the manufacturing process (confidential), impurity profiles (confidential), hazard data available to FAO/WHO, and the manufacturer’s name and address remain valid. Proposers are responsible for notifying FAO/WHO of changes in this information. If the validity of this information is in doubt, the specification(s) may be scheduled for review by the JMPS. Manufacturers of products evaluated by WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES), upon which WHO recommendations for use and specifications are based, must notify WHO of any changes to the manufacturing process, formulation characteristics, or formulants that could require re-evaluation of the product and/or review of the specification. Proposers may also request a review of specifications. The JMPS will then confirm whether the existing specification is suitable, recommend an amended specification, or recommend that the specification be withdrawn. In cases where a specification serves as a reference for equivalent products and needs revision, an amendment or modification of a clause may render previously equivalent products non-equivalent. In such situations, JMPS submits a draft version of the revised specification for consultation to data proposers with equivalent products. If new data are needed to support continued equivalence, an appropriate deadline for submission of the data is set. When national authorities find it necessary to adapt FAO or WHO specifications, FAO and WHO should be informed by the proposer or the authority of the changes made and the reasons for them. Such modified specifications cannot be considered FAO/WHO specifications, but information supporting the changes will assist JMPS in revising the specifications. Comments and further information relating to specifications are welcomed by FAO and WHO. Proposals for modification of specifications should be supported by evidence showing that the change is relevant to maintaining or improving the quality/performance or reducing the risks of the technical grade active ingredient or formulation. Data requirements for specifications include the name, address, and contact point of the proposer(s), the draft new specification or a statement of the specification to be extended, and any other relevant information likely to help JMPS make sound recommendations. All clauses in the draft specification should be presented in a standard form. Analytical methods supporting FAO and WHO specifications for determining active ingredients in technical and formulated pesticides must be collaboratively tested and approved by CIPAC or AOAC. Peer-validation data should be submitted to AOAC or CIPAC to support the adoption of the method. If validation data have not yet been considered by CIPAC or AOAC, FAO/WHO may request submission of the data for preliminary review. Physical test methods may be validated by CIPAC, ASTM, or according to the requirements of OECD or EC, or, where appropriate, by equivalent pharmaceutical organizations. References to physical test methods in this Manual are prefixed with “MT” for CIPAC methods, “EC” for European Community methods, or the complete acronym for OECD or ASTM methods. These methods are considered definitive as, in many cases, the physical property is defined by the method of measurement. Where more than one method is available, a referee method must be designated. Validation requirements for methods determining unstable physical properties, which are not amenable to validation by collaborative study, are currently under consideration by CIPAC. Until defined by CIPAC or equivalent, the validation requirements will be determined by FAO/WHO on a case-by-case basis. Although the level of acceptance of methods within the CIPAC or AOAC systems is not completely critical, preference is given to “full” or “final action” methods, and methods should normally have achieved at least “provisional” or “first action” status. The absence of an agreed and published specification guideline does not preclude submission of a proposed specification. FAO and WHO encourage the development of novel formulations addressing pest control problems. For unique formulation types, the manufacturer must define the critical characteristics and provide suitably validated test methods for measuring the appropriate parameters.
